c.tagline: A Norman cathedral crowning a wooded river peninsula, where medieval stone meets student life.

taxi.color: No mandated uniform colour — mostly black, silver, or white saloon/estate hackney carriages licensed by Durham County Council
taxi.fare: £4.90 flagfall (covers first mile/8 min) + ~£2.40/mile daytime; £6.30 flagfall + ~£3.30/mile nights (10pm-7am), Sundays and bank holidays
taxi.fareNote: Taxis are exempt from the city centre's congestion charge; fixed fare to Newcastle Airport is roughly £45-50 (~$60-67 USD)

emergency.note: Durham is consistently ranked among the UK's safer cities. Main risks are petty theft (bikes, unattended bags) and weekend alcohol-related disorder around the Walkergate/Elvet bar area; violent crime against visitors is rare.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Late-night weekend rowdiness around North Road and the club streets; otherwise usual awareness.

hood_desc: The medieval heart of Durham, occupying the peninsula almost entirely owned by the University and Cathedral. Cobbled lanes, Palace Green, the Castle, and the Cathedral itself dominate this pedestrianised core — the obvious base for first-time visitors.

Across the river via Elvet Bridge, this area (including Walkergate and Old Elvet) is Durham's main nightlife and dining district, home to student pubs, Klute nightclub, and riverside restaurants, plus the county courts and Dunelm House.

A quieter, largely residential conservation area west of the river with independent cafes, vintage/arts spaces like the Empty Shop, and views back across the Wear to the Cathedral from the Victorian viaduct.
A mixed residential and retail neighbourhood east of the centre, home to the medieval St Giles' Church, the Gilesgate retail park, and Sainsbury's superstore — practical rather than picturesque.

A leafy residential suburb southwest of the centre, near the site of the 1346 Battle of Neville's Cross, within walking distance of Durham University's Botanic Garden and Observatory — a calm, green alternative base.
lodging: Delta Hotels by Marriott Durham Royal County

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the UK.

transit.hours: Local buses generally run about 6am-11pm (reduced Sunday service); Park & Ride roughly 7:15am-8pm Monday-Saturday
transit.pay: Contactless card/Apple Pay tap-and-go on buses with daily fare caps, or a Park & Ride return ticket (around £3) bought on-site or via app
transit.map: Traveline North East app/website for journey planning, plus individual Arriva and Go North East apps
transit.note: The historic peninsula has restricted vehicle access and a congestion charge for cars entering the centre; walking or using the Park & Ride is strongly recommended over driving in.

train: Durham Station (East Coast Main Line; LNER to London, Edinburgh and Newcastle)
bus: National Express coaches connect Durham to London (roughly 6-7 hours) and other major UK cities
Regional buses run from Durham bus station on North Road via Arriva and Go North East

airport.name: Newcastle International Airport
airport.note: ~20 miles (32 km) north of Durham. Tyne and Wear Metro links the airport directly to Newcastle Central Station (about 25 minutes), then a mainline train to Durham (about 12-15 minutes); direct taxi/private hire fixed fare is roughly £45-50 (~$60-67 USD), about 30-35 minutes.

transit.m: Tyne and Wear Metro to Newcastle Central, then train to Durham (about 50 min)

tip.s: Tipping isn't obligatory in the UK; rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service (bars, taxis, cafes) is appreciated but never expected.
tip.r: 10-12.5% is standard for sit-down restaurant service if a service charge isn't already added — check the bill first, as many Durham restaurants add it automatically for groups.

places.name: Bells Fish Shop

food.desc: Small-batch gin distilled in the county, botanical-heavy and usually served long with local tonic; the city's answer to the craft spirits boom.

places.name: Coviello

landmarks: Durham Cathedral
Britain's finest Norman building, a UNESCO masterpiece holding the shrines of St Cuthbert and the Venerable Bede above the wooded River Wear.
Durham Castle
The 11th-century motte-and-bailey fortress of the prince-bishops, now University College, tours its Norman chapel, great hall and Tunstall gallery.
Palace Green
The tranquil lawn between cathedral and castle, ringed by medieval university buildings and the Palace Green Library's exhibitions, is Durham's postcard core.
River Wear Riverbanks Walk
Wooded towpaths loop the river's incised meander beneath the cathedral, with rowing boats for hire and iconic views from Prebends Bridge.
Framwellgate Bridge
A medieval stone crossing of about 1400 framing the classic composition of castle and cathedral stacked above the Wear.
Durham Market Place and Market Hall
The bustling historic square, watched by the Neptune statue and Lord Londonderry's equestrian monument, adjoins a Victorian indoor market of independent stalls.
Crook Hall and Gardens
A romantic medieval hall wrapped in themed English gardens, moments from the city centre and now cared for by the National Trust.
Oriental Museum
Durham University's treasure house of Asian and Egyptian art, from Chinese jade and Japanese prints to mummies, unique in northern England.
Elvet Bridge
A 12th-century bridge built by Bishop Puiset, once lined with chapels and a house of correction, linking the peninsula to old Elvet.
Finchale Priory
Golden sandstone ruins of a 13th-century Benedictine priory curl into a peaceful loop of the Wear, a short riverside trip downstream.

train.note: No international trains - change in London for Eurostar. Durham sits on the East Coast Main Line with a spectacular viaduct approach: LNER trains reach London King's Cross in about 2h50, Edinburgh in 2h, Newcastle in 12 minutes and York in 45 minutes. The station is a steep ten-minute walk above the city. Advance fares open 12 weeks out.

bus.note: No direct international coaches. National Express (https://www.nationalexpress.com/) stops at North Road bus station with services to London and the north, and Go North East runs the frequent local buses to Newcastle, Sunderland and the Durham Dales. The train is much faster for Newcastle.

ferry.note: Durham is inland on a loop of the River Wear, which carries rowing boats and short cruises but no scheduled service. The nearest international crossing is DFDS's overnight ferry from North Shields near Newcastle to IJmuiden for Amsterdam, about 40 minutes north.

half.name: Newcastle upon Tyne
half.blurb: Tyneside city of bridges and riverside quaysides, with a lively bar scene and the Baltic and Sage Gateshead arts venues.

half.name: Beamish Museum
half.blurb: Open-air living history museum recreating a 1900s pit village, tram lines, and a working coal mine you can descend.

half.name: Hadrian's Wall
half.blurb: UNESCO Roman frontier wall stretching across northern England, with forts and museums accessible around Hexham and Housesteads.

full.name: Whitby
full.blurb: North Yorkshire coastal town with a ruined clifftop abbey that inspired Dracula, a working harbor, and steep cobbled streets.

full.name: Holy Island (Lindisfarne)
full.blurb: Tidal island with a ruined priory and Lindisfarne Castle, reachable only via a causeway that floods with the tide.

notes.walk: Compact and highly walkable — the historic core sits on a wooded peninsula formed by a horseshoe bend of the River Wear, with the Cathedral and Castle crowning the top. Expect steep cobbled lanes and stairs since Durham is built on hills, but nearly every major sight is within a 15-20 minute walk of Market Place. Vehicle access to the peninsula is restricted (congestion charge for cars), keeping the centre pedestrian-friendly.
notes.card: Card and contactless payment (including Apple/Google Pay) is the norm almost everywhere, from cafes to buses; cash is rarely needed but useful for small independent stalls at the indoor market.
notes.safety: Durham is regularly rated one of the safest cities in the UK, with crime well below the national average, and is popular with solo travelers, students, and families. Petty theft (bike theft, unattended bags) and alcohol-related disorder around the Walkergate/Elvet nightlife strip on weekend nights are the main concerns; violent crime against tourists is rare. Use standard precautions after dark near the station underpass and pub-crawl routes.
notes.religion: Christian 53.5%; No religion 39.3%; Not stated 5.2%; Muslim 0.7%; Other religions 1.3%
notes.net: Good 4G/5G coverage across the city centre and peninsula from all major networks, though signal can weaken on rural approach roads. Widely available free wifi in cafes, pubs, the university library, and Durham's public libraries; most hotels and B&Bs include free wifi. A 1-month PAYG SIM with 10-20GB typically costs $15-25 (£12-20). Free wifi is common in cafes, pubs, and public buildings; ask staff for the network password. A UK/EU eSIM or local PAYG SIM (available at Newcastle Airport or supermarkets) is advisable for stays longer than a few days.
notes.transit: Arriva North East and Go North East operate local buses; Durham also runs a dedicated Park & Ride service (Belmont, Howlands, and Sniperley sites) feeding the city centre
notes.transport: Nearest airport is Newcastle International (NCL), about 20 miles north, roughly 45-60 minutes away via Tyne and Wear Metro plus train, or by taxi/car. Durham station sits on the East Coast Main Line with frequent LNER services: London King's Cross in about 2h50m-3h, Edinburgh in about 1h45m, and Newcastle in just 10-15 minutes. National Express coaches connect Durham to London (roughly 6-7 hours) and other major UK cities; regional buses run from Durham bus station on North Road via Arriva and Go North East. N/A — Durham is inland with no ferry access; the nearest ferry port is at North Shields near Newcastle (DFDS to Amsterdam), about 20 miles away. Durham sits just off the A1(M) motorway; the central peninsula has restricted, charged vehicle access, so park at a Park & Ride site or city car park and walk in.
